en: The Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings, translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmagatayaśas of India during the Xiao Qi period.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in the city of Rājagṛha.
He was accompanied by a great assembly of twelve thousand bhikṣus,
eighty thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, as well as bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.

Great wheel-turning kings, minor wheel-turning kings, and all other wheel-turning kings of the golden and silver wheels; kings, princes, state ministers, citizens, scholars, ladies of the realm, and great householders—each surrounded by retinues numbering in the hundreds of thousands of millions—came to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at his feet, circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times, and made various offerings of burning incense and scattered flowers.
Having made these offerings to the Buddha, they withdrew to sit to one side.
The bodhisattvas were named Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, Mahāteja-garbha Kumārabhūta, Aśoka-garbha Kumārabhūta,
Mahāpratibhāna-garbha Kumārabhūta, Maitreya Bodhisattva, Nāyaka Bodhisattva,
Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva, Bhaiṣajyasamudgata Bodhisattva, and Puṣpakūṭa Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Flower-Radiance Banner, the Bodhisattva Sovereign King of Dhāraṇīs,
the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, the Bodhisattva Constantly Diligent, the Bodhisattva Jewel-Seal Hand,
the Bodhisattva Jewel-Heap, the Bodhisattva Jewel-Staff, the Bodhisattva Transcender of the Three Realms, and the Bodhisattva Vimalavara.
Sattva, Gandhahastin Bodhisattva, Mahāgandhahastin Bodhisattva, Siṃhanādavikrāmin Bodhisattva,
Siṃhavikrīḍitalokamitra Bodhisattva, Siṃhavijṛmbhita Bodhisattva,
Siṃhavikrāntagāmin Bodhisattva, Parākramabala Bodhisattva, Siṃhaparākramavinardita Bodhisattva, and Alaṃkāra Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Great Adornment, and eighty thousand other such Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas were present together.
Among these Bodhisattvas, there was not one who was not a Great Being of the Dharma-body, perfected in morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.

Their minds are tranquil in dhyāna, constantly abiding in samādhi; they are serene, peaceful, and detached, being unconditioned and free from desire. Perversions and distracted thoughts can no longer enter them; they are still, silent, pure, and clear, with their will fixed upon the profound and vast void. Maintaining this without wavering for hundreds of thousands of koṭis of kalpas, immeasurable Dharma-gates all appear before them.

Having attained great wisdom, they penetrate all dharmas, clearly understanding and discerning the reality of natures and characteristics, existence and non-existence, long and short, making these manifest and luminous.

Furthermore, they are well able to know the faculties, dispositions, and desires of others. Through dhāraṇīs and unhindered eloquence, they entreat the Buddhas to turn the wheel of Dharma, turning it in accordance with the needs of beings. Like the first falling of a drop of rain that quenches the dust of desire, they open the gate of nirvāṇa, fan the wind of liberation, remove the world’s feverish afflictions, and bring about the coolness of the Dharma.
Next, he brings down the profound twelve links of dependent origination to douse the fierce and blazing sun of the mass of suffering—ignorance, old age, sickness, death, and so forth.

Thereupon, he pours forth the unsurpassed Mahāyāna, moistening the roots of goodness within all sentient beings and sowing seeds of virtue throughout the field of merit. He causes all to sprout the bud of Bodhicitta; through the sun and moon of wisdom and the seasonal conditions of skillful means, he nurtures and increases the activities of the Mahāyāna, enabling the multitude to swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and abide eternally in bliss, subtlety, and reality.

Possessing immeasurable great compassion, they rescue suffering sentient beings; they are the true spiritual friends of all sentient beings, the great and excellent fields of merit for all sentient beings, the uninvited teachers of all sentient beings, and the place of peace and happiness for all sentient beings. They are the place of rescue, the place of protection, and the place of great reliance, acting as great guides for the masses everywhere.

They can serve as eyes for those born blind, providing ears, noses, and tongues for those who are deaf, noseless, or mute; they can cause those with impaired faculties to become complete, and provide great right mindfulness to those who are deranged or disordered.
As captains and great captains, they transport the multitudes of living beings across the river of birth and death, establishing them on the shore of nirvana.

The King of Physicians, the Great King of Physicians, discerns the characteristics of diseases and understands the nature of medicines; he administers medicine according to the ailment so that all may take it with joy.

He is the Tamer, the Great Tamer, free from all heedless conduct; like a master of elephants and horses, he can tame all who are untamed. Like a lion, he is courageous and fierce, subduing all other beasts, and is impossible to thwart or destroy.

Sporting in the various *pāramitās* of a bodhisattva, remaining firm and unshakable in the stage of a Tathāgata, and dwelling securely in the power of their vows, they extensively purify buddha-fields and will before long attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
All these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess such inconceivable merits.

Among them were the bhikṣus named Mahāmati Śāriputra, the supernaturally empowered Maudgalyāyana, the venerable Subhūti, Mahākātyāyana, Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, Ājñātakauṇḍinya, and others; as well as Aniruddha with his divine eye, Upāli the upholder of the Vinaya, the attendant Ānanda, the Buddha’s son Rāhula, Upananda, Revata, Kapphiṇa, Bakula, Acchuta, Śagata, Mahākāśyapa the great dhūta-practitioner, Uruvilvākāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, and Nadīkāśyapa.

There were twelve thousand bhikṣus such as these, all of whom were arhats; they had exhausted all fetters and outflows, were free from further bondage and attachment, and had attained true liberation.

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāvyūha surveyed the entire assembly; once everyone had settled their minds, he rose from his seat together with eighty thousand Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas from among the multitude. They approached the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrated themselves at his feet, and circumambulated him a hundred thousand times. They scattered celestial flowers, celestial incense, celestial robes, celestial necklaces, and priceless celestial jewels from the air as they descended in spirals, gathering like clouds from all four directions to present offerings to the Buddha.

Celestial kitchens, celestial bowls, and celestial vessels were filled to overflowing with a hundred celestial flavors; by merely seeing their colors or smelling their fragrance, one was naturally satiated.
Celestial banners, celestial pennants, celestial canopies, and exquisite celestial musical instruments were installed everywhere.
They performed celestial music to entertain the Buddha.
Then, they came forward and knelt with their right knees on the ground; with palms joined and single-minded devotion, they spoke these verses of praise in unison:
"How great is the Great Awakening, O Great Holy Lord! Stainless, undefiled, and free from all attachment!"
The Teacher who tames gods, humans, elephants, and horses, His Way’s wind and virtue’s fragrance permeate all.
Wisdom is tranquil, emotions stilled, and anxieties settled; Thought ceases, consciousness vanishes, and the mind is likewise silent.
Forever severed are dreams, delusions, ideations, and memories; No longer exist the aggregates, elements, or sense-bases.
That body is neither existent nor non-existent; It is neither cause nor condition, neither self nor other;
Neither square nor round, neither short nor long; Neither emerging nor submerging, neither arising nor ceasing;
Neither created nor produced, neither fashioned nor contrived; Neither sitting nor lying, neither walking nor standing.
Neither moving nor turning, neither still nor tranquil; Neither advancing nor retreating, neither secure nor perilous;
Neither right nor wrong, neither gain nor loss; Neither that nor this, neither going nor coming;
Neither blue nor yellow, neither red nor white; Neither crimson nor purple—none of these manifold colors.
Precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation arise; the three clarities, the six supernormal powers, and the factors of the path emerge;
compassion, the ten powers, and the fearlessnesses are produced; all these issue from the causes and conditions of the virtuous karma of sentient beings.
He manifests as one sixteen feet tall, with the luster of purple-gold; his form is square and regular, radiating a most brilliant clarity.
His *ūrṇā* curls like the moon, and his neck emits the light of the sun; his hair swirls in deep blue-black, and his crown is adorned with a fleshy protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*).
His pure eyes shine brightly, blinking up and down; his eyebrows and eyelashes are a deep azure, and his mouth and cheeks are well-proportioned.
His lips and tongue are as red and beautiful as cinnabar fruits; his forty white teeth are like jade or snow.
His forehead is broad, his nose long, and his face is open and radiant. Upon his chest is the svastika mark, and his breast is like that of a lion.
His hands and feet are soft and supple, marked with the thousand-spoked wheel; the webbing between his fingers and toes is joined like a seal, extending both inward and outward.
His arms are long and his elbows reach down; his fingers are straight and slender. His skin is fine and soft, with body hairs curling to the right.
His ankles and knees do not protrude, and his private parts are concealed like those of a horse. His sinews are fine and his clavicles are distinct; his calves are like those of a deer.
He is transparent from within and without, pure and free of defilement; like clear water, he cannot be stained and receives no dust.
Such are the thirty-two marks and the eighty minor signs that may be seen;
yet in reality, they are markless and not of the nature of form. All things with marks are beyond the reach of the eye;
this markless mark is the body with marks, and the bodily marks of sentient beings are likewise so.
They cause sentient beings to rejoice and pay homage, With a devout heart expressing sincere and earnest respect;
Because of this, self-exaltation and pride are eliminated, And they achieve such a body of wondrous form.
We, a multitude of eighty thousand, together bow our heads and take refuge in you,
the Noble One who has well extinguished thought, mind, and consciousness, the unattached Master who tames like an elephant or a horse.
I prostrate and take refuge in the Dharma-body of form, the aggregate of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
I prostrate and take refuge in the wondrous banner-mark; I prostrate and take refuge in the inconceivable.
The Brahma-voice thunders with eight qualities, subtle, pure, profound, and far-reaching;
following the minds and karmic actions of sentient beings, it turns toward the Four Truths, the Six Perfections, and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination.
All who hear it find their minds opened, and the immeasurable fetters of birth and death are severed.
Some hear of it or attain the stage of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, or arhat;
the state of the untainted, unconditioned pratyekabuddha; and the bodhisattva stages of non-arising and non-ceasing.
Some attain immeasurable dhāraṇīs and unimpeded, joyful eloquence of great discernment;
they expound profound and subtle verses, sporting and bathing in the pure pond of the Dharma.
Sometimes leaping and soaring, manifesting supernormal powers;
appearing and disappearing in water and fire with bodily mastery—such are the characteristics of the Dharma wheel, pure, boundless, and inconceivable.
We all together prostrate once more, taking refuge in the turning of the Wheel of Dharma at the proper time.
We prostrate and take refuge in the Brahma-like voice; we prostrate and take refuge in the conditions, the truths, and the perfections.
In the past, throughout immeasurable eons, the World-Honored One diligently practiced all virtuous deeds for the sake of humans,
devas, dragon kings, and spirit kings, extending his grace universally to all sentient beings.
Able to relinquish all that is difficult to give— wealth, treasures, wife, children, and kingdoms—
without begrudging anything internal or external regarding the Dharma, they bestow even their heads, eyes, marrow, and brains upon others;
upholding the pure precepts of all Buddhas, they do not violate them even at the cost of their lives.
If someone comes to inflict harm with sword or staff, Or insults and reviles with foul speech, he never feels anger;
Throughout kalpas, he endures physical mortification without weariness, Day and night restraining his mind, ever abiding in dhyāna;
He studies all the various paths and dharmas extensively, His wisdom penetrating deeply into the faculties of sentient beings.
Therefore, having now attained the power of mastery, you are the Dharma King who exercises sovereignty over all phenomena;
we all together prostrate ourselves and take refuge in you, who are able to persevere where others find it difficult to persevere.

Chapter Two: Exposition of the Dharma. At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Great Adornment, together with eighty thousand Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, having spoken these verses in praise of the Buddha, addressed the Buddha in unison, saying:
“World-Honored One!

"We, a multitude of eighty thousand bodhisattvas, now wish to inquire about certain matters within the Dharma of the Tathāgata; we do not know whether the World-Honored One will compassionately deign to grant us an audience."
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāvyūha and the eighty thousand bodhisattvas, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"Good son! You know well the proper time; ask whatever you wish.
Before long, the Tathāgata shall enter parinirvāṇa, and after his nirvāṇa, he will cause all beings to be free from any further doubt."
"Whatever you wish to ask, you may speak it.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Mahāvyūha and eighty thousand bodhisattvas spoke with one voice to the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to swiftly attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), what dharma-gates should they practice?
What dharma-gates can cause a bodhisattva mahāsattva to swiftly attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāvyūha and the eighty thousand bodhisattvas, saying:
“Sons of good family!
There is a dharma-gate that enables a bodhisattva to swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
"If there are bodhisattvas who study this dharma-gate, they will be able to swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"World-Honored One!
What is the name of this dharma-gate?"
"What is the meaning of this?
How should a bodhisattva practice?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! This Dharma-gate is called ‘The Immeasurable Meanings.

A bodhisattva who wishes to practice and study the immeasurable meanings should observe that all dharmas, from their very origin until now, are empty and quiescent in their essential nature and characteristics; they are neither large nor small, neither arising nor ceasing, neither abiding nor moving, and neither advancing nor retreating.”

Just as space is devoid of duality, sentient beings falsely and arbitrarily conceptualize "this" and "that," "gain" and "loss. Giving rise to unwholesome thoughts, they commit various evil karmas and transmigrate through the six realms, undergoing all manner of bitter poisons; for immeasurable billions of kalpas, they are unable to escape on their own.
When the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates in this manner, he gives rise to a heart of compassion, arouses great loving-kindness and pity, and intends to rescue and deliver [beings].

Furthermore, he penetrates deeply into all phenomena (*dharmas*): that the characteristic of phenomena is such, that such phenomena are produced; that the characteristic of phenomena is such, that they abide in such phenomena; that the characteristic of phenomena is such, that they differ from such phenomena; that the characteristic of phenomena is such, that such phenomena cease.

That the characteristic of phenomena is such, that they can produce unwholesome phenomena; that the characteristic of phenomena is such, that they can produce wholesome phenomena; and that it is likewise for their abiding, changing, and ceasing.

“When a bodhisattva has thus observed the beginning and end of these four characteristics and has fully understood them, they next contemplate all phenomena with clear discernment: that they do not abide for even a single moment, but arise and perish anew at every instant.”
Furthermore, he contemplates arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing at that very moment; having contemplated thus, he enters into the faculties, dispositions, and inclinations of sentient beings.
Because their inclinations and desires are immeasurable, his preaching of the Dharma is immeasurable;
because the preaching of the Dharma is immeasurable, its meanings are also immeasurable.
That which is of immeasurable meaning arises from a single dharma;
that single dharma is precisely signlessness (*animitta*).
Such signlessness—wherein signlessness is not a sign, and non-sign is signlessness—is called the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

Once the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is established in such true reality, the compassion they generate is clear, certain, and not in vain; toward sentient beings, they are truly able to uproot their suffering.
Once suffering has been uprooted, he further preaches the Dharma for them, causing all sentient beings to experience happiness. "Good son!
If a bodhisattva can thus cultivate the immeasurable meanings within a single dharma-gate, they will certainly swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi."
“Good son!

This profound and unsurpassed Mahāyāna *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* is authentic in its principles and elegant in its phrasing; it is supreme and beyond compare. It is protected by all Buddhas of the three periods of time, such that no hosts of Māras or followers of heterodox paths can enter it, nor can it be destroyed or defeated by any false views or the cycle of birth and death.”
Therefore, good son!
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to swiftly attain unexcelled bodhi, they should practice and study this profound and unsurpassed Mahāyāna *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāvyūha again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The World-Honored One’s teaching of the Dharma is inconceivable; the faculties and natures of sentient beings are also inconceivable; and the liberation of the Dharma-gates is likewise inconceivable.”
"We have no further doubts regarding the various dharmas spoken by the Buddha; however, because sentient beings give rise to deluded minds, we ask again.
World-Honored One!"

Since the Tathāgata attained the Way more than forty years ago, he has constantly expounded for the sake of sentient beings the meaning of the four marks of all dharmas: the meaning of suffering, the meaning of emptiness, impermanence, and non-self; that there is no large and no small, no arising and no ceasing; that all things are without marks; and that the nature and characteristics of dharmas are fundamentally empty and quiescent—neither coming nor going, neither emerging nor vanishing.
If there are those who hear it, some will attain the stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*), the stage of Summits (*mūrdhan*), or the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*);
others will attain the fruit of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), the fruit of Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), the fruit of Non-returner (*anāgāmin*), or the fruit of Arhat;
and still others will attain the path of a Pratyekabuddha.
They have resolved their minds on Bodhi and ascended through the first, second, third, and up to the tenth stage.

What difference is there between the meaning of the various dharmas you previously taught and those you now teach, that you say this *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings of the Profound and Unsurpassed Mahāyāna* ensures that a bodhisattva who practices it will necessarily and swiftly attain unsurpassed Bodhi?
What is the meaning of this matter?

We only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion for all, will explain it in detail for the sake of sentient beings, so that those who hear the Dharma in the present and future ages may be freed from every net of doubt.
Thereupon, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāvyūha:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"O Great Son of Good Family!

Since you are able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding such profound, unsurpassed, and subtle meaning of the Mahāyāna, you should know that you are capable of bringing great benefit, peace, and happiness to humans and devas, and of uprooting suffering for sentient beings; you truly possess great compassion, and your faith is sincere and not false."
By these causes and conditions, one will surely and swiftly attain unexcelled bodhi, and will also cause all sentient beings in the present and future lives to attain unexcelled bodhi.

“Good son! Since I sat upright for six years beneath the Bodhi tree at my place of enlightenment and attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I have observed with the Buddha-eye that all dharmas are ineffable.”
Why is this? Because the dispositions and desires of sentient beings differ.
Since their dispositions and desires differ, the Dharma is taught in various ways.
Through various modes of teaching and the power of skillful means, for more than forty years he has never revealed the ultimate truth.
For this reason, sentient beings attain different paths and are unable to swiftly achieve unsurpassed bodhi.
Good son!
The Dharma is like water, which can wash away defilements; whether it be from a well, a pond, a river, a stream, a brook, a canal, or the great ocean, all are able to cleanse every kind of impurity.
The water of that Dharma is likewise: it can wash away the defilements of the afflictions of sentient beings. Good son!
The nature of water is one and the same, yet rivers, streams, wells, ponds, brooks, channels, and the great ocean each differ from one another.
The nature of these dharmas is likewise so: they wash away afflictions without distinction; thus, the three dharmas, the four fruits, and the two paths are not one.
"Good son!

Although water is equally cleansing, a well is not a pond, a pond is not a river or a stream, and a mountain brook or a canal is not the ocean; likewise, the Tathāgata, the Hero of the World, possesses mastery over all dharmas, and the various teachings he proclaims are also like this."

The teachings given at the beginning, middle, and end are all capable of washing away the afflictions of sentient beings; yet the beginning is not the middle, and the middle is not the end. Although the phrasing of the teachings given at the beginning, middle, and end is identical, their meanings differ in each case.

“Good son! When I rose from beneath the King of Trees and went to the Deer Park at Vārāṇasī to turn the Wheel of the Dharma of the Four Truths for the five men, including Ājñātakauṇḍinya, I also taught that all dharmas are originally empty and quiescent, undergoing successive change without abiding, arising and ceasing in every thought-moment.

In the interval, here and in various other places, for the sake of the bhikṣus and the assembly of bodhisattvas, I have expounded and proclaimed the twelve links of dependent origination and the six pāramitās; therein too, I have taught that all dharmas are originally empty and quiescent, undergoing successive change without abiding, arising and ceasing in every thought-moment.”

Now, once again here, I expound the Mahāyāna *Anantārthasūtra*, wherein I also teach that all dharmas are originally empty and quiescent, undergoing constant change without abiding, arising and ceasing from moment to moment.
"Good son! Therefore, what was spoken at the beginning, what was spoken in the middle, and what is spoken now, are identical in their phrasing, yet differ in their meaning.
Because the meanings differ, the understandings of sentient beings differ."
Because their understandings differ, the attainment of the Dharma, the attainment of the fruit, and the attainment of the Path also differ. "Good son!
When the Four Truths were first preached for those seeking the state of a śrāvaka, eight hundred million devas descended to listen to the Dharma and gave rise to the bodhicitta."

In various places, he expounded the profound twelvefold chain of dependent origination for those seeking the state of a pratyekabuddha; thereby, immeasurable sentient beings resolved their minds upon bodhicitta, or entered the stage of śrāvakas.

Next, he expounded the Vaipulya sūtras of the twelve divisions, the Mahāprajñāpāramitā, and the Flower Ornament Sea-Cloud, proclaiming the bodhisattvas’ cultivation through successive kalpas; thereby, hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus, ten trillion humans and devas, and immeasurable sentient beings attained the stage of Srotāpanna, attained the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin, attained the stage of Anāgāmin, attained the stage of Arhat, and dwelt within the causal conditions of the Pratyekabuddha Dharma.
Good son! For this reason, you should know that while the expressions are the same, their meanings are distinct.
Because the meanings differ, the understandings of sentient beings differ.
Because their understandings differ, the dharmas they attain, the fruits they realize, and the paths they follow also differ.
Therefore, good son!

From the time I first attained the Way and began to preach the Dharma until this day as I expound the Mahāyāna *Anantārtha Sūtra*, there has never been a time when I have not spoken of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self; that things are neither real nor false, neither great nor small; that they were originally not so and now do not perish; that all are without marks, and that the characteristics and nature of dharmas neither come nor go, yet sentient beings are still transmuted by the four marks.
“Good son! For this reason, the Buddhas have no double speech; they can respond universally to all voices with a single sound;
and they can manifest from a single body hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of immeasurable and innumerable bodies, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.”
Within each and every body, he further displays hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas, asaṃkhyeyas, and Ganges-sand-like varieties of forms;
within each and every form, he further displays hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas, asaṃkhyeyas, and Ganges-sand-like forms.
"Good son!

This is the inconceivable and profound realm of all Buddhas; it is not something known by those of the Two Vehicles, nor can it be reached by Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes. Only Buddhas, with Buddhas, are able to fully comprehend it."

“Good son! For this reason, I have preached the subtle, profound, and unsurpassed Mahāyāna *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*. Its principles and expressions are authentic and correct, its honor is supreme and beyond compare; it is protected by all Buddhas of the three periods of time. No demons or non-Buddhists can enter it, nor can it be destroyed or defeated by any wrong views or the cycle of birth and death.”
If Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas wish to swiftly attain unsurpassed enlightenment, they should practice and study this profound and unsurpassed Mahāyāna *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*.
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, this trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and spontaneously from the sky there rained down various flowers:
celestial *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* blossoms;

furthermore, there rained down countless varieties of celestial incense, celestial garments, celestial necklaces, and priceless celestial jewels, which whirled down from the sky above to make offerings to the Buddha, as well as to the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.
Celestial kitchens, celestial bowls, and celestial vessels were filled to overflowing with the hundred flavors of heaven;

celestial banners, celestial pennants, celestial canopies, and celestial musical instruments were set out everywhere, whereupon celestial music was performed and songs of praise were sung for the Buddha.

Furthermore, there were six kinds of earth tremors. In the Buddha-worlds of the eastern direction, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there likewise rained down celestial flowers, celestial incense, celestial garments, celestial necklaces, and priceless celestial jewels; celestial kitchens, celestial bowls, celestial foods of a hundred flavors, celestial banners, celestial pennants, celestial canopies, and exquisite celestial musical instruments. Celestial music was performed, singing praises of those Buddhas, as well as those Bodhisattvas and the great assemblies of Śrāvakas.
It was likewise so in the southern, western, and northern directions, the four intermediate points, and the zenith and nadir.
Thereupon, thirty-two thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas among the assembly attained the Samādhi of Immeasurable Meaning;

thirty-four thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attained countless and immeasurable dhāraṇī-doors, whereby they were able to turn the non-retrogressive wheel of Dharma of all Buddhas of the three periods of time. As for those bhikṣus...
bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas,
asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, great wheel-turning kings, minor wheel-turning kings, silver-wheel kings, iron-wheel kings, and all other wheel-turning kings;
When the king, princes, ministers, citizens, gentlemen, ladies, great elders,
and their retinues of hundreds of thousands heard the Buddha, the Tathāgata, preach this sutra, some attained the stage of Heat (uṣmagata), the stage of Summits (mūrdhan),
the stage of the World’s Foremost Dharma (laukikāgradharma), or the fruit of Stream-entry (srotāpattiphala).
The fruit of the Sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of the Anāgāmin, the fruit of the Arhat, and the fruit of the Pratyekabuddha;
furthermore, they attain the bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);
furthermore, they attain one dhāraṇī, two dhāraṇīs, three dhāraṇīs, four dhāraṇīs, five, and six.
...the seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth *dhāraṇīs*, and further attained hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *dhāraṇīs*,
and furthermore attained immeasurable, incalculable, *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka-asamkhyeya* *dhāraṇīs*.
They were all able to follow and turn the irreversible wheel of Dharma, causing immeasurable sentient beings to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Three: The Bodhicitta.
Chapter Three: The Ten Merits. At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāvyūha again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
The World-Honored One has preached this subtle, profound, and unsurpassed Mahāyāna *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*, which is truly profound!
It is most profound, most profound! Why is this so?

Within this assembly, all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the fourfold assembly—gods, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, kings, ministers, subjects, and all other sentient beings—who heard this profound and unsurpassed Mahāyāna *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*, there were none who did not attain the gates of dhāraṇī, the three dharmas, the four fruits, and the mind of enlightenment.

You should know that this sutra is authentic in both principle and expression, supreme and unsurpassed; it is protected by the Buddhas of the three periods of time, such that no host of Māras or followers of heterodox paths can enter it, nor can it be destroyed or defeated by any wrong views or the cycle of birth and death.
Why is this? Because one who hears it once is able to uphold all dharmas.
If there are sentient beings who manage to hear this sutra, they will obtain great benefit.
Why is this? If one is able to practice it, one will certainly and swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

As for those sentient beings who do not hear it, you should know that they have lost a great benefit; for immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) kalpas, they shall ultimately never attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Why is this? Because they do not know that the Great Path to Bodhi is direct, they travel along perilous byways where obstacles abound.
World-Honored One!
This sutra is inconceivable.
We only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion for the great assembly, will extensively expound upon the profound and inconceivable matters of this sutra.
World-Honored One!
From where does this sutra come?
To where does it go?
In what state does he abide,
such that he possesses these immeasurable merits and inconceivable powers, enabling sentient beings to swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Great Adornment, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Good son! It is so, it is so, just as you have said. Good son!"
I say that this sutra is most profound, most profound!
It is truly profound! Why is this so?

It is for the sake of causing the multitude to swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; because one can uphold all dharmas upon hearing them once; because it brings great benefit to all sentient beings; and because one practices the great direct path without hindrance.
"Good son!
As for your question regarding where this sutra comes from, where it goes to, and where it abides—listen attentively and with care.
Good son!"

This sutra originally comes from the palaces of all Buddhas; it goes forth to reach all sentient beings who have resolved to attain bodhicitta, and it dwells in the spheres of practice of all bodhisattvas.
"Good son! This sutra comes in this way, goes in this way, and abides in this way.
Therefore, this sutra possesses such immeasurable merit and inconceivable power that it enables sentient beings to swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Good son!
Would you like to hear that this sutra further possesses ten inconceivable powers of merit?
Mahāvyūha replied:
“I wish to hear it with joy.
The Buddha said, “Good son!
First, this sutra is able to cause bodhisattvas who have not yet resolved their minds to generate the bodhicitta;
to cause those who lack compassion and benevolence to give rise to a compassionate mind;
and to cause those who delight in slaughter to give rise to great compassion.
Toward those who give rise to jealousy, one should arouse a mind of sympathetic joy;
toward those who possess attachment, one should arouse a mind capable of renunciation;
and toward all those who are stingy and greedy, one should arouse a mind of giving.
For those with much arrogance, they give rise to the mind of upholding the precepts;
for those with abundant anger and hatred, they give rise to the mind of patience;
for those who have become indolent, they give rise to the mind of diligence.
For those who are distracted, they give rise to a mind of meditative concentration;
for those who are ignorant, they give rise to a mind of wisdom;
for those who have not yet crossed over, they give rise to a mind to deliver them.
For those who practice the ten unwholesome deeds, they give rise to the mind of the ten wholesome deeds;
for those who delight in the conditioned, they set their will upon the unconditioned mind;
for those with regressive minds, they cultivate the non-regressive mind.
For those with outflows, they give rise to the outflow-free mind;
for those with many afflictions, they give rise to the mind that eradicates them. Good son!
This is called the first inconceivable power of the merit of this sutra. "Good son, secondly, as for the inconceivable power of the merit of this sutra:

if there are sentient beings who obtain this sutra—even a single turning, a single verse, or even a single phrase—they will be able to penetrate hundreds of thousands of billions of meanings, such that they could not fully expound the Dharma they have received and upheld even throughout immeasurable kalpas."
Why is this? Because the meaning of this Dharma is immeasurable. Good son!

This sutra is like a single seed from which hundreds of thousands of millions grow, and from each of those hundreds of thousands of millions, yet again hundreds of thousands of millions are produced; thus it continues in succession until they become immeasurable.

This scripture is also like this: from a single dharma, hundreds of thousands of meanings arise, and from each of those hundreds of thousands of meanings, yet again hundreds of thousands of millions are produced; thus it continues in succession until there are immeasurable and boundless meanings.
Therefore, this sutra is titled "The Immeasurable Meanings.
Good son! This is called the second inconceivable power of the merit of this sutra.

“Good son! Thirdly, regarding the inconceivable power of merit of this sutra: if there are sentient beings who hear this sutra—even a single turning, a single verse, or even a single phrase—and having mastered hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of meanings, then although they possess afflictions, they are as if without afflictions; they enter birth and death without thoughts of fear; they give rise to a heart of compassion toward all sentient beings; and they attain a sense of courageous strength regarding all dharmas.”
Just as a strong man is able to carry and support all that is heavy;

so too is this person who upholds the sutra: they are able to bear the precious burden of unsurpassed bodhi, carrying sentient beings across the path out of birth and death. Though they have not yet attained liberation themselves, they are already able to deliver others.

It is just as if a boatman were afflicted by a grave illness, his four limbs unable to function, remaining on this shore; yet he possesses a fine, sturdy vessel and constantly prepares all the equipment for crossing others over, providing it to them before departing.

So too is it with the holder of this sutra: although they are embodied within the various existences of the five realms, perpetually entangled by the hundred-and-eight grave illnesses, and remain on this shore of ignorance, old age, and death, they possess this firm and great Mahāyāna sutra of immeasurable meaning, prepared to enable the crossing of sentient beings.
Those who are able to practice according to what has been taught will attain liberation from birth and death.
Good son! This is called the third inconceivable power of the merit of this sutra.

“Good son! Fourth, regarding the inconceivable power of merit of this sutra: if there are sentient beings who hear this sutra—even a single turning, a single verse, or even a single phrase—and conceive a sense of courageous strength, they will be able to deliver others even though they have not yet delivered themselves; they will become companions to all bodhisattvas, and all Buddhas and Tathāgatas will constantly expound the Dharma for such persons.”
Having heard this, such a person is able to receive and uphold it entirely, following it without opposition, and further explains it extensively for others as appropriate. Good son!

Such a person is like a prince newly born to a king and queen; whether after one day, two days, or up to seven days; or one month, two months, or up to seven months; or one year, two years, or up to seven years—though he is still unable to manage the affairs of state, he is already revered by his ministers and subjects, takes the other great princes as his companions, and the king and queen hold him with particular affection, constantly speaking with him.
Why is this? Because they are young and immature. Good son!
It is the same for this upholder of the sutra: the Buddhas are the kings, this sutra is the queen, and through their harmonious union, they together give birth to this son, the bodhisattva.

If a bodhisattva hears this sutra—even a single sentence, a single verse, one turning, or two turnings; or ten, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred million, a billion, or as many turnings as there are sands in the Ganges, immeasurable and incalculable—they shall, though unable yet to realize the ultimate limit of true reality, and though unable yet to shake the trichiliocosm or produce the thunderous Brahma-sound while turning the Great Dharma Wheel, already be venerated by all fourfold assemblies and the eight classes of beings, have the great bodhisattvas as their retinue, penetrate deeply into the secret teachings of all Buddhas, and in whatever they expound, be without contradiction or error. They shall always be protected and remembered by all Buddhas, who will cover them with exceptional compassion because they are but newly initiated students.
"Good son! This is called the fourth inconceivable power of the merit of this sutra. Good son!"

Fifth, regarding those who possess the inconceivable power of merit: if a son of good family or a daughter of good family—whether while the Buddha is in the world or after his parinirvāṇa—should receive, uphold, read, recite, or transcribe such a profound and unsurpassed Mahāyāna *Anantārtha Sūtra*, this person, though still bound by all afflictions (*kleśa*) and unable yet to distance themselves from the affairs of ordinary beings, can manifest the path of great bodhi. They can extend a single day to last for a hundred kalpas, and likewise condense a hundred kalpas into a single day, causing those sentient beings to rejoice, believe, and submit.
Good son! These good sons and good daughters are like dragon princes who, having been born for only seven days, are immediately able to raise clouds and also able to send down rain.
“Good son! This is called the fifth inconceivable power of the merit of this sutra. Good son!”

Sixth, regarding the inconceivable power of merit of this sutra: if a son of good family or a daughter of good family, whether while the Buddha is in the world or after his parinirvāṇa, receives, maintains, reads, and recites this sutra, then although they possess afflictions, they shall preach the Dharma for sentient beings, enabling them to distance themselves from afflictions and birth-and-death, and to sever all suffering.
When sentient beings hear this and practice accordingly, they attain the Dharma, attain the fruit, and attain the Way, becoming equal to the Buddha-Tathāgata without any distinction.
It is like a prince who, though still young, is entrusted with the governance of state affairs by the king when the king goes on tour or falls ill.

At that time, the prince, in accordance with the Great King’s command, instructed the various ministers and officials according to the Dharma to propagate the true transformation; thus, the people of the land each attained peace according to their station, no different from the governance of the Great King himself.

It is the same for the sons and daughters of good family who uphold this sutra: whether the Buddha is in the world or has entered parinirvāṇa, these sons of good family, although they have not yet attained the first Immovable Stage (akṣobhyabhūmi), expound the teachings according to the manner in which the Buddha thus taught them. When sentient beings hear them, they practice with single-minded devotion, severing their afflictions (kleśa) and attaining the Dharma, the fruits, and even the Path.
"Good son! This is called the sixth inconceivable power of the merit of this sutra. Good son!"

Seventh, regarding those who possess the inconceivable power of merit from this sutra: if a son of good family or a daughter of good family, whether while the Buddha is in the world or after his parinirvāṇa, hears this sutra and with joy, faith, and delight gives rise to a sense of rarity, and then receives, upholds, reads, recites, copies, explains, and practices it according to the Dharma; if they resolve for bodhicitta, give rise to various roots of goodness, and arouse great compassion with the desire to deliver all suffering and distressed sentient beings—then even if they have not yet practiced the six pāramitās, the six pāramitās will naturally appear before them. They shall immediately attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) in that very body, sever and destroy birth, death, and afflictions all at once, and ascend to the seventh stage, attaining the rank of a Great Bodhisattva.
For example, suppose a capable man eliminates an enemy for a king; once the enemy has been destroyed, the king is greatly delighted and bestows upon him a fief equal to half the kingdom as a reward.

The men and women who uphold this sutra are likewise so: they are the most courageous and steadfast among all practitioners; the jewel-treasure of the six perfections comes to them spontaneously without being sought; the enemies of birth and death naturally disperse and perish; they realize the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); and they receive the peace and bliss of the half-share of the Buddha-land as their reward.
"Good son! This is called the seventh inconceivable power of the merit of this sutra. Good son!"

Eighth, regarding the inconceivable power of merit of this sutra: if a good man or a good woman, whether during the Buddha’s lifetime or after his parinirvāṇa, should obtain this sutra, they should revere and believe in it as if beholding the Buddha’s own body, regarding it as equal and no different from him. They should cherish this sutra, receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, copying, and wearing it upon their heads; they should practice according to the Dharma, remain firm in precepts and patience, concurrently practice the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), and deeply give rise to loving-kindness and compassion, extensively expounding this unsurpassed Mahāyāna *Anantārthasūtra* for others.

If there are those who have previously never believed in the existence of sin and merit, one should show them this sutra and employ various skillful means to strengthen their resolve until they believe. By the power of the sutra, their minds are awakened and they suddenly achieve a transformation of heart.
Once faith has arisen, through their courageous and diligent application, they are able to attain the majestic power and influence of this sutra, thereby realizing the Way and its fruits.

Therefore, good sons and good daughters shall, in this very body, attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), ascend to the higher stages, and become the retinue of all bodhisattvas; they will swiftly be able to bring sentient beings to maturity and purify buddha-fields, and before long, they will attain unsurpassed bodhi.
"Good son! This is called the inconceivable power of the eighth merit of this sutra. Good son!"
Ninth, regarding the inconceivable power of merit of this sutra: if any son of good family or daughter of good family—
whether while the Buddha is in the world or after his parinirvāṇa— should obtain this sutra and experience unprecedented joy and exultation,
and should receive, uphold, read, recite, transcribe, and make offerings to it, and extensively [expound it] for others...
Those who analyze and explain the meaning of this sutra shall have the remaining karmic offenses and heavy obstructions from their past lives extinguished all at once;
they will immediately attain purity, achieve great eloquence, successively adorn themselves with the various pāramitās,
obtain all samādhis— including the Śūraṅgama Samādhi— and enter the Great Dhāraṇī.

Having entered this gate, one attains the power of diligent vigor and swiftly transcends the higher stages; one is well able to emanate bodies and disperse forms throughout the lands of the ten directions,
rescuing all sentient beings suffering in the twenty-five realms of existence and causing them all to attain liberation.
Therefore, this sutra possesses such power. Good son!
This is called the ninth inconceivable power of the merit of this sutra.

“Good son! Tenth, regarding the inconceivable power of merit of this sutra: if a good man or a good woman—whether while the Buddha is in the world or after his parinirvāṇa—should obtain this sutra and give rise to great joy and a sense of rare wonder, and then personally uphold, read, recite, copy, make offerings to, and practice according to its teachings; and furthermore, if they can widely exhort householders and renunciants to uphold, read, recite, copy, make offerings to, explain, and practice according to the Dharma; and having caused others to practice, those who thereby attain the Way and its fruits do so entirely through the power of the compassion and diligent transformation of these good men and good women.”

These sons and daughters of good family shall, in this very body, immediately attain immeasurable gateways of dhāraṇī. At the very beginning of their stage as ordinary beings, they are able to give rise to countless asaṃkhyeya great vows of universal resolve; they are deeply capable of vowing to rescue all sentient beings, achieving great compassion and extensively saving those from suffering. They amass roots of goodness in abundance to benefit all, spreading the moisture of the Dharma to generously nourish the parched and wither. Using the medicinal herbs of various dharmas, they refine all sentient beings, bringing peace and happiness to all, so that they may gradually ascend and dwell upon the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma (Dharmameghā-bhūmi). Their grace and favor universally moisten all, their kindness extends beyond all bounds, and they gather in suffering beings, causing them to enter the tracks of the Path.
Therefore, this person will before long attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Good son! This is called the tenth inconceivable power of the merit of this sutra.

“Good son! This unsurpassed Mahāyāna *Anantārthasūtra* possesses exceedingly great majestic spiritual power; it is most honored and unsurpassed, capable of enabling all ordinary beings to attain the fruits of sainthood, forever leaving birth and death behind to achieve mastery.”
For this reason, this sutra is titled "The Teaching of Immeasurable Meanings.

It enables all sentient beings, while still on the stage of ordinary persons, to give rise to the immeasurable sprouts of the bodhisattva path, causing the tree of merit to flourish, spread its branches, and grow.
"Therefore, this sutra is titled 'The Ten Inconceivable Powers of Merit.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Great Adornment and eighty thousand Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas addressed the Buddha with one voice, saying:
'World-Honored One!'"

The *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*, spoken by the Buddha, is profound, subtle, and unsurpassed Mahāyāna; its principles and phrasing are authentic and correct, and it is most venerable, beyond compare. It is protected by all Buddhas of the three periods of time, such that no hosts of Māras or followers of heterodox paths can enter it, nor can it be destroyed or defeated by any wrong views or the cycle of birth and death.

Therefore, this sutra possesses such ten kinds of inconceivable power of merit, which brings great benefit to all immeasurable sentient beings, causing all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to each attain the samādhi of immeasurable meanings, or to obtain hundreds of thousands of dhāraṇī gates, or to attain the various stages (bhūmi) and patiences (kṣānti) of the bodhisattvas, or to realize the fruits of the four paths of the pratyekabuddhas and arhats.
The World-Honored One, out of compassion, has most excellently expounded such a Dharma for us, enabling us to obtain great benefit from the Dharma; this is truly extraordinary and unprecedented.
"The compassionate grace of the World-Honored One is truly difficult to repay.
At that time, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and from the sky above there fell a rain of various flowers:
celestial *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* blossoms.

Furthermore, countless varieties of celestial incense, celestial garments, celestial necklaces, and priceless celestial jewels rained down from the sky, swirling as they descended to make offerings to the Buddha, the bodhisattvas, and the great assembly of śrāvakas. Celestial kitchens, celestial bowls, and celestial vessels filled with a hundred flavors overflowed; upon seeing their colors or smelling their fragrance, all were spontaneously satiated. Celestial banners, celestial pennants, celestial canopies, and celestial musical instruments were set up everywhere, where celestial music was performed and songs were sung in praise of the Buddha.

Furthermore, there were six kinds of earth tremors. In the Buddha-worlds of the eastern direction, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, there likewise rained down celestial flowers, celestial incense, celestial robes, celestial necklaces, and priceless celestial jewels; celestial kitchens, celestial bowls, and celestial foods of a hundred flavors appeared. Upon seeing their colors and smelling their fragrances, beings were spontaneously satisfied. There were also celestial banners, celestial pennants, celestial canopies, and exquisite celestial musical instruments, which played celestial music and sang praises of those Buddhas, as well as the assemblies of Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas. The same occurred in the southern, western, and northern directions, as well as in the four intermediate points and the zenith and nadir.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Great Ornament (Mahāvyūha) and the eighty thousand Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, saying:

"You all should conceive a profound heart of reverence for this sutra, practice according to the Dharma, extensively transform all beings, and diligently disseminate it. You must always be earnestly vigilant in guarding it day and night, so that all sentient beings may universally obtain the benefits of the Dharma."

"You all possess true great kindness and great compassion; by establishing the power of your supernatural vows, you shall protect this sutra so that it does not become obstructed by doubt. In future ages, you must cause it to be widely disseminated throughout Jambudvīpa, so that all sentient beings may see, hear, recite, transcribe, and make offerings to it."
"For this reason, I shall also cause you all to swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāvyūha, together with eighty thousand Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas, rose from their seats and approached the Buddha. They prostrated themselves at his feet, circumambulated him a hundred thousand times, and then knelt before him with their right knees on the ground. In unison, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
We have been greatly blessed by the World-Honored One’s compassion, as he has expounded for our sake this profound, subtle, and unsurpassed Mahāyāna *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*.

Respectfully accepting the Buddha’s command, we shall, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, cause this sūtra to be widely disseminated, so that all may universally uphold, recite, copy, and make offerings to it.
We only pray that the World-Honored One will not harbor any anxiety.

By the power of our vows, we shall cause all sentient beings everywhere to see, hear, read, recite, copy, and make offerings to this sutra and its Dharma, so that they may obtain the majestic spiritual power of this teaching.
At that time, the Buddha praised him, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"O sons of good family!
You who are now truly the children of the Buddha possess great kindness and great compassion, and are deeply capable of uprooting suffering and rescuing those in distress.

You are the excellent field of merit for all sentient beings; you act as great and virtuous guides for all; you are the great place of reliance for all sentient beings; you are the great benefactors for all sentient beings, constantly bestowing the benefits of the Dharma extensively upon everyone."
At that time, the entire great assembly was filled with immense joy; they prostrated before the Buddha, received and upheld [the teaching], and departed.
*The Sutra of Immeasurable Meanings* (Wúliàngyì jīng).
